title: P99 surge: scheduling + contention analysis and hotfix validation
content:
Summary:

On 2026-04-11 we received a high-severity escalation from Customer X reporting intermittent P99 latency spikes for generative chat endpoints. The customer saw 2–4x increases in P99 during peak windows, causing UI timeouts and a support SLO breach. This doc captures the investigation, root cause, the emergency mitigations we shipped, and validation steps with telemetry and customer confirmation.

Impact and scope:
- Affected: Customer X chat endpoints (model: rdx-7b-int8-optim) in prod-eu1 only
- Window: 2026-04-11 09:20–12:10 UTC (recurrent short bursts across the window)
- Observed: baseline p99 ~420 ms → spikes up to ~1.8 s; p95 increased modestly from 170 ms → 260 ms
- Traffic: correlated with customer traffic patterns (many small user messages concurrently), but other tenants with similar QPS did not show equivalent spikes
- Business: customer reported degraded UX and opened urgent support ticket; internal SLO alert fired.

Initial triage (first 90 minutes):
- Slack thread: #cust-escalations -> engaged on-call runtime + SRE + SE
- Quick Grafana checks: CPU/GPU utilization steady; GPU SM utilization moderate; host-level CPU steal low
- Queues: serving runtime's short-request queue saw bursts and transient backlog; per-GPU request queue depth spiked by up to 6x during events
- KV-cache and model weights cold starts were ruled out (no high coldstart rate, models pinned)
- Hypotheses prioritized: scheduler fairness/backpressure bug, CUDA stream contention, kernel selection fallback to slower path for int8 at certain sequence lengths.

Profiling and evidence gathered:
- Lightweight flamegraphs collected from the hot path during spike windows (see Flamegraph link). Key signals:
  - Large fraction of wall-clock in scheduler->dispatch path (merge/assign logic) during spikes (~35% of p99 stack vs ~8% at baseline)
  - Increased time spent in CUDA stream synchronization calls (cudaStreamSynchronize) suggesting cross-stream blocking
  - Kernel invocation latency distribution widened for the int8 attention kernel: median unchanged, but a long tail where certain kernels took 3–5x longer
- Trace-level sampling (1% requests) showed many requests were split into multiple micro-batches by the scheduler even when their batch compatibility allowed coalescing
- NVLINK throughput (host-level perf counter) had short bursts matching latency spikes indicating intermittent cross-GPU traffic pressure when many tiny batches were dispatched in rapid succession
- A small but reproducible codepath in the kernel selector: for sequence lengths in [128, 160] the selector preferred a vectorized int8 kernel marked "experimental" which under heavy small-batch parallelism caused L2 thrashing and higher latency. This selector path was exercised often by Customer X's message length distribution.

Root cause (synthesized):
A compound of three interacting factors produced the P99 surge:
1) Scheduler micro-batching heuristics were too eager to split compatible requests across multiple execution quanta to optimize throughput; this increased the number of concurrent small kernels launched across CUDA streams.
2) The kernel selector had an optimistic experimental int8 kernel path for the customer's common seq lengths that degenerates under high inter-stream contention (L2 cache thrash + memory traffic), producing a long-tail kernel latency for a subset of invocations.
3) The increased concurrent kernel launches caused transient NVLINK saturation for cross-GPU KV cache fetches in certain configurations, amplifying the per-request tail.

Why this hit Customer X and not others:
- Their workload had many small, independent chat messages (avg tokens/request ~24) concentrated in the vulnerable seq length window that triggered the experimental kernel selector path frequently.
- Other tenants either triggered stable kernels or had larger average batch sizes so the scheduler coalescing behaved differently.

Immediate mitigations (hotfix):
- Hotfix PR (#2187) rolled within 3 hours (staged to prod-eu1):
  1) Modify scheduler to prefer coalescing compatible small requests into a single micro-batch when per-GPU queue depth > 4 (conservative gating to avoid throughput regressions)
  2) Disable the experimental int8 attention kernel selector for the seq-length range [112, 192] (falls back to the stable int8 kernel path)
  3) Add short-circuit backpressure: if NVLINK transfer counters exceed threshold X for >200 ms, throttle concurrent dispatch to allow cooldown
- Configuration was feature-flagged and A/B tested on 6% of prod-eu1 traffic for 30 minutes before full rollout.

Validation / results:
- Observed immediate reduction in p99 spikes in prod-eu1: p99 returned to 420–520 ms during the previous spike window (baseline variance returned).
- Scheduler queue depth spikes reduced by ~70% during peak windows in A/B test clusters.
- Kernel tail events (long kernel invocations) dropped by ~92% after disabling experimental kernel for the seq range.
- End-to-end customer confirmation: Customer X ran their repro script; they reported stable experience and no further UI timeouts after the fix.

Follow-ups and action items (owners):
- Runtime: revisit scheduler micro-batching policy and implement adaptive coalescing based on recent latency feedback (owner: Samir Gupta) — RFC due 2026-04-26
- Inference-ML: audit kernel selector heuristics and add stress tests for multi-stream small-batch scenarios; re-evaluate experimental kernels under realistic parallel load (owner: Lena Ortiz) — plan due 2026-05-03
- SRE: add a Grafana panel for NVLINK cross-GPU transfer counters with alert thresholds; instrument end-to-end traces to include kernel-selection metadata (owner: Marcus Li) — complete by 2026-04-22
- QA: add synthetic replay tests that mimic Customer X request-size distribution into nightly regression suite (owner: Priya Rao) — test added by 2026-04-20
- Customer Success: follow up with Customer X and offer a technical post-call and a short educational note on recommended batching patterns (owner: [CS] Naomi Chen) — scheduled 2026-04-16

Lessons learned:
- Compound interactions between scheduler heuristics and opportunistic kernel paths can produce brittle tail behavior; we need more integration-style stress tests that exercise multi-stream small-batch concurrency with real token length distributions.
- Feature-flagging experimental kernels and gating them behind cluster-scale stress tests would have caught this earlier.
- Telemetry: adding kernel-selector labels to traces made root-cause identification much faster; we should standardize this labeling across runtime telemetry.

Appendix (data excerpts):
- Baseline / spike latencies (prod-eu1, Customer X):
  - 2026-04-11 09:00–09:20: p50 98 ms, p95 170 ms, p99 420 ms
  - 2026-04-11 09:20–09:40 (spike period): p50 110 ms, p95 250 ms, p99 1800 ms
  - Post-hotfix (2026-04-11 13:00–14:00): p50 105 ms, p95 180 ms, p99 475 ms
- Synthetic microbenchmark: 1k concurrent small requests (avg tokens 24)
  - Before: median kernel latency 1.9 ms, 99th kernel latency 14.8 ms (when experimental path hit)
  - After: median kernel latency 2.1 ms, 99th kernel latency 3.1 ms (stable path)

Notes to reviewers:
- Attached artifacts (Flamegraph, Grafana) contain the raw traces used for this analysis. Please check the scheduler logs (trace IDs in linked artifacts) if you need to reproduce the window.
- We intentionally used a conservative scheduler coalescing gate to avoid throughput regressions during the hotfix; the longer-term adaptive approach should allow more aggressive coalescing when it is safe.

Acknowledgements:
Thanks to on-call SRE Marcus Li for the quick NVLINK perf counters, QA Priya Rao for rapid repro harnesses, and ML infra lead Lena Ortiz for kernel selector review.

End of report.
